name: Cosmopolitanism (the idea of mankind as a whole)
plain_explanation: Once Alexander began treating Greeks and non-Greeks as potential equals -- marrying Persian nobility, ordering his officers to do the same, founding mixed cities -- thoughtful people started to conceive of humanity as one community rather than a patchwork of rival city-states and superior/inferior races.
precise_definition: The view that human loyalty and moral concern extend, in principle, to all mankind rather than being confined to one's own city or ethnic group; in philosophy this view is first fully worked out by the Stoics.
why_it_mattered: Russell treats it as the single most important social legacy of Alexander's reign, and as the historical seed of Stoic universalism and, later, of Christian and modern conceptions of a common humanity.
historical_origin: Emerges in practice from Alexander's policy of fusion (intermarriage, mixed garrison-cities) after his conquests, before it is formulated in theory.
associated_philosopher: Alexander the Great (in practice); the Stoics (in theory, treated in Ch. XXVIII)
examples: Alexander's own marriages to Persian princesses
His compelling his Macedonian officers to marry Persian noblewomen
Greek cities founded throughout Asia with mixed populations
objections: Plato and Aristotle had held it wrong to enslave Greeks but not barbarians -- the older, particularist view cosmopolitanism displaced
competing_positions: The traditional Greek view of a sharp superiority over 'barbarians', which Russell quotes Aristotle as expressing
influence_on_later_thinkers: Directly anticipates the Stoic doctrine of the brotherhood of man (Ch. XXVIII) and, through the Stoics, later Christian and Roman legal ideas of natural human equality (Ch. XXIX).
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Political in origin (imperial policy of fusion), later absorbed into philosophy and religion.
